extracted.intended_audience: readers and investigators of alleged fossil/antiquities finds; general educated public and scientific examiners
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating whether a discovered 'fossil' or ancient statue is genuine or a modern fabrication, using physical, chemical, taphonomic, provenance, and testimonial evidence. Includes awareness of common hoax fabrication techniques and staged-examination tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material–environment chemical consistency (gypsum solubility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the material of the object is chemically compatible with the claimed burial environment and time (example: 'gypsum is soluble in 400 parts of water, yet the surface of the giant was smooth and little dissolved, though surrounded by wet earth, proving that the burial must have been of very recent date').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare known solubilities and weathering rates of the material (e.g., gypsum) with observed state; unexpected preservation given the burial conditions suggests recent manufacture or burial. Use controlled dissolution/weathering expectations as a test of antiquity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of recent tool-marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Look for signs of recent tooling on the surface (explicitly cited: 'recent tool-marks, in places where they could not be easily effaced').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspect surfaces at appropriate magnification for fresh chisel, saw, or other tool marks that are inconsistent with long-term burial or natural erosion. Recent, sharp tool-marks adjacent to supposedly water-worn surfaces are a red flag.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency between surface treatments (water-worn) and other marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Check whether water-worn appearance coexists plausibly with other surface evidence (e.g., tool-marks adjoining water-worn surfaces were noted as inconsistent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be skeptical when 'water-worn' surfaces are present alongside fresh tool-marks or other signs of recent manufacture; such juxtaposition often indicates artificial aging (e.g., rubbing with sand and water to simulate antiquity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Artificial surface ageing techniques (sand/water rubbing, pecking, chemical baths)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify signs of deliberate artificial ageing methods described on the page: long rubbing with sand and water to produce water-worn appearance; pecking the surface with leaden hammers faced with needles to imitate pores/'goose-flesh'; bathing with writing-fluid and washing with sulphuric acid to remove 'fresh' appearance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for microscopic patterns characteristic of man-made abrasion, uniformity of marks, residues of modern chemicals, and signs of localized treatment. Knowledge of these known hoaxing techniques helps interpret suspicious surface features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal structure/contents (crystals, inserted bones, fillers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine internal composition (e.g., natural crystals expected in fossilized material; hoaxers may insert 'crystal dust' or fragments of skull/bones in specific locations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use boring, cross-sectioning, X-ray, or CT scanning to inspect internal matrix. Natural fossilization tends to produce characteristic crystalline structures; deliberate insertion or substitution (crystal dust, bone fragments placed to deceive) can be detected by inconsistency, placement, or composition analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taphonomic/anatomical plausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether anatomical features and expected taphonomic changes fit the alleged mode of preservation (examples: 'rotundity incompatible with the theory of one who had died and become fossilized, in which case the abdomen would naturally be sunken and collapsed'; lack of hair when otherwise complete).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare the specimen's morphology to expected post-mortem deformation and preservation patterns for the claimed context. Implausible anatomy given taphonomy suggests fabrication or misinterpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provenance and chain-of-custody scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate documentary and eyewitness evidence about discovery and transport (the text cites witnesses to a four-horse team hauling the object, drafts payable to the fabricator, and receipts of payment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain independent accounts of discovery, transport, and transactions. Contradictory or compromising provenance (e.g., money drawn payable to the maker, observed transport shortly before 'discovery') is strong evidence of fraud. Corroborate or refute claims with contemporaneous records and witnesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition analysis for modern binders and materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze material composition for modern constituents used in fabrication (examples of hoax recipes given: ground stone, pulverized bones, clay, plaster, blood, dried eggs, baked in a kiln).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laboratory chemical and microstructural analyses (petrography, organic residue testing, microscopy) can detect modern adhesives, organics, or manufacturing signatures inconsistent with natural fossilization or ancient production techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of restricted or staged examinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Be cautious if finders insist that examiners may only test limited parts ('we propose to let the scientific men bore into him, but they must confine themselves to certain parts of his body, and there we have fixed him by putting in bones').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require unrestricted, systematic examination; beware of conditions that channel tests to pre-prepared areas. Staged limitations on inspection are a common tactic to prevent detection of fraud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek appropriately qualified, independent experts
rubrics_metrics.description: Rely on assessments by relevant specialists (e.g., geologists, archaeologists, sculptors) rather than unqualified local practitioners—text notes differing opinions from medical men, geologists, sculptors, and university scientists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assemble a multidisciplinary, independent team for evaluation. Cross-check conclusions from sculptors (tooling and stylistic assessment), geologists (material and taphonomy), and chemists (composition). Be wary of paid or biased experts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine documentary and testimonial contradictions among promoters
rubrics_metrics.description: Use internal disputes, confessions, or inconsistent statements among those involved (examples: admissions of Cox, Case, Babcock, etc., who later fell out and exposed the scheme) as evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect and scrutinize statements by participants and stakeholders; conflicting accounts, admissions, or evidence of collusion strengthen suspicions of fabrication and can provide leads to provenance and methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corroborate physical tests with contextual/archaeological expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine physical/chemical results with broader archaeological and contextual expectations (e.g., geographic plausibility, absence/presence of analogous finds, expected burial contexts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anomalous finds should be evaluated against known regional archaeological record and plausible depositional contexts. Extraordinary claims require multiple lines of consistent evidence (materials, taphonomy, context, provenance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of common hoax incentives and patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider motivations (financial gains from exhibitions, publicity) and repeated patterns (fabrication methods reused across hoaxes) as part of the assessment ('Hull cleared some 160,000 by the latter, with which he embarked in business...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the discovery fits known incentive structures (commercial exhibition, publicity) and known hoax techniques; such sociological/contextual factors inform the likelihood of fraud and guide investigative priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of visible transportation/handling evidence as diagnostic
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for physical evidence of recent handling or transport that contradicts antiquity claims (e.g., iron-bound case, apparent weight requiring significant motive power, recent movement observed by witnesses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine packaging, tool marks on crates/cases, fresh sawdust, and other signs of recent transport; trace logistics (shipping records, station arrivals) to corroborate or refute claims of in-situ discovery.
